name: Adam Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This interview is confidential, including anything different from what you'd say publicly. Could you describe your normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Adam, 43, a junior electrician with a vocational certificate. I prepare wiring runs and help with home and business repairs, but I'm still less skilled than the experienced crew and need a senior check. This morning I took too long sorting the fittings for a kitchen and had to ask which circuit the drawing referred to. I enjoy finally understanding a job, even if I get there later than everyone else.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life around the job like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner runs a small curtain-repair service, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. My wage is typical for the trade, and we have two months of expenses saved, but curtain orders have been thin recently; there are some other electrical firms nearby. I use AI occasionally for job notes after a colleague has shown the tool works, not to decide what I'm qualified to do. I value apprenticeships, work and family help, and I'd rather compare a real paid place than chase a promise about a safe new career.

say: I'd welcome **less machine talk** while accepting quicker office invoices.
I'd still ask for **senior checks** on my practical work regardless of how clever the office tools became.
think: My **steady wage** doesn't remove worry while my partner's curtain orders remain thin.
Two months of **expenses saved** can shrink quickly against a mortgage and the children's ordinary needs.
do: Cancel the optional **sports package** now and use its cost for household bills.
Continue **supervised repairs** during the first year rather than risk the wage on an uncertain scheme.
Ask my brother about one **school pickup** if it enables a confirmed curtain job.
feel: **Anxious** about household income, despite relief that his own electrical wage continues.
S0.quote: A steady wage isn't the same as a steady household income.
fieldNote: His **baseline worry** follows current partner-income uncertainty alongside a moderate reserve, rather than an assumed AI threat to all practical work.
The **family request** is limited to an actual booking and remains unconfirmed; he doesn't count a possible favour as dependable childcare.

steps.text: Cancel the optional sports package and use its cost for bills
Continue supervised electrical repairs through the first plateau year
Ask the brother for one pickup enabling a confirmed curtain job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a bit less noise about machines would suit me. If the office made invoices quicker, I wouldn't object. I'd still want the senior worker to check my work, however clever the office became.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd worry about the household money even if AI barely changed the job. My wage is steady, but my partner's orders are thin, and two months of expenses can shrink quickly with the mortgage and children. A steady wage isn't the same as a steady household income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd cancel the optional sports package and put that cost towards the household bills. In the first plateau year I'd keep doing supervised repairs rather than leave a steady wage for an uncertain scheme. I'd ask my brother whether one agreed school pickup a week was possible if it helped my partner take a confirmed curtain job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household, not about the note tool. I'd feel relieved the electrical work carried on but still listen carefully whenever my partner said an order had been cancelled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain the spending cut at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the actual monthly cost rather than announce we were giving up every small pleasure. We'd keep the children's regular school needs ahead of the extra television channels. It's a modest cut, not a replacement for missing orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you count on your brother taking over childcare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd ask about one particular afternoon when an actual customer booking existed. My brother has his own work, and he could say no. We wouldn't count a possible favour as a childcare plan already in place.

say: I'd try **proven tools** while asking the firm to keep time for teaching juniors.
I'd separate using a **checked assistant** from having practical experience I haven't yet gained.
think: My practical hours may continue, but **less teaching** could keep me learning slowly on the same wage.
The household still faces **thin curtain orders**, with mortgage payments unaffected by faster office booking.
do: Learn the **AI note assistant** from a senior worker using an old completed job now.
Use it only in **paid work** during the first year, with checked output, while retaining the sports-package cut.
feel: **Anxious** about household money and progression, while willing to try a tool already proved useful.
S1.quote: I can learn a checked tool without pretending it makes me an experienced electrician.
fieldNote: His **tool use** remains occasional and follows a senior worker's proof, fitting his steady approach without upgrading junior competence.
The **household baseline** persists alongside slower learning concerns; a request for paid teaching hasn't become course enrollment or a provided place.

steps.text: Learn the proven AI note assistant only during paid work with senior checks
Keep the optional sports package cancelled to reduce bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should use a tool once someone has proved it helps the actual work. I'd also want the firm to keep time for teaching juniors rather than fill every saved minute with another call. I can learn a checked tool without pretending it makes me an experienced electrician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own practical hours probably continue, but less senior time could leave me learning more slowly and stuck at the same pay. I'd still have the thin curtain orders in the household account. Faster booking wouldn't change the mortgage date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the senior worker to show me the AI note assistant on an old completed job without customer details. In the first year I'd use it only during paid work, with the senior checking the result. I'd keep the sports-package cut and ask for paid practical teaching time with no loss of site wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household and whether I could progress, but willing to try something already checked. I wouldn't feel overwhelmed by the software. I'd be more worried about a week with no time to ask a basic question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the senior worker had no time left to teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what had been agreed about teaching and whether one paid session a week was possible. If the answer was no, I wouldn't pay for an evening course from money the household needed. I'd look at actual apprenticeship vacancies before making any bigger choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the assistant produced an inaccurate job note?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop using that output and show the senior worker the mismatch. A clean-looking note that described the wrong work wouldn't help anybody. I'd rather send a checked simple note than an impressive wrong one.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 thinking changes** from robots around 2031 and seek a paid route before both stages.
I'd ask what **wage arrives** during the gap rather than treating three years as automatic security.
think: My **junior hours** could shrink as firms prepare for robots and concentrate practical work among experienced people.
The **two-month reserve** gives only a short search while the household still needs my mortgage contribution.
do: Ask the old instructor about actual **paid apprenticeships** with supervised practical teaching now.
Accept a supervised **apprenticeship place** only if its written wage covers household bills after travel.
Apply after 2028 for posted **junior repair work** with workable written wages, staying until a signed offer.
feel: **Anxious** about a realistic income cut, with a reserve and places to ask providing some control.
S2.quote: I'd prefer work and apprenticeship to support, but that preference doesn't let me invent a wage.
fieldNote: He describes **possible income loss** without certainty of total wage loss, making anxiety consistent with his remaining control and resources.
His **apprenticeship preference** doesn't erase affordability, supervision or the option to check actual lender and support arrangements if income falls.

steps.text: Take supervised paid apprenticeship only with wages covering bills after travel
Apply after 2028 for junior repair work with workable written wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew to keep 2028 thinking changes separate from robots following around 2031. I'd still want a proper paid apprenticeship route before that second date. Three years sounds useful until you ask what wage arrives during it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose junior hours as firms prepared for capable hands-on machines and kept the experienced people busy. Our two-month reserve would give us a short search, not support the mortgage indefinitely. I wouldn't know that the whole wage was going, but I would worry about a real cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask my old instructor for actual supervised paid-apprenticeship vacancies, not just course advertisements. I'd take one before 2028 only if the written wage covered household bills after travel and teaching was properly supervised. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply for posted junior repair work on the same basis, keeping the present job until a signed offer existed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with the household pressure sharper than in the plateau. I would still have places to ask and a little reserve. I wouldn't feel it was certain disaster, but I wouldn't call it an adventure either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you discuss with your partner before accepting an apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the wage, hours, journey and teaching arrangement before calling it an opportunity. If the household couldn't live on the actual money, I'd keep looking. I'd prefer work and apprenticeship to support, but that preference doesn't let me invent a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no affordable paid place was available and income fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If our income fell, we'd ask the lender about real options before missing a payment and check any support eligibility without assuming approval. I'd talk with my partner rather than silently try to carry every worry. Family responsibility includes saying when the numbers don't work.

say: I'd use **five years** to seek real paid learning places now instead of waiting until 2031.
I'd keep the **2034 hands-on change** in view while asking employers to make supervised practice possible.
think: More time could improve my **practical skill** before robot competition pressed directly on electrical work.
Today's **uncertain partner income** and two-month reserve still leave the household financially anxious.
do: Maintain the **sports-package cut** and ask the instructor about actual paid apprenticeship places now.
Accept a supervised **apprenticeship** before 2031 only with written wages covering bills after travel.
Apply after 2031 for posted **junior service work** where written pay and hours improve the household position.
feel: **Anxious** about present household money, with less pressure to learn the practical trade at an impossible speed.
S3.quote: I'd want useful work, not a growing pile of attendance papers.
fieldNote: The **longer preparation** improves skill prospects without solving the partner-income uncertainty established before any scenario was read.
He refuses **unaffordable training** and judges progress against correctly performed work and actual vacancies, keeping the current wage meanwhile.

steps.text: Keep the sports package cancelled to reduce household bills
Take supervised apprenticeship only with wages covering bills after travel
Apply after 2031 for junior service work with better written pay and hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us room to learn properly while we're paid, if employers make the places real. I'd still ask about those places now rather than wait for 2031. The hands-on robots around 2034 would remain part of the same picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with 2028, I'd have longer to become useful before direct robot competition pressed on the work. But my partner's orders are still uncertain now, and our reserve is only two months. Extra learning time would help me without making this month's household income secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the sports-package cut and ask the instructor about real paid apprenticeship places. I'd accept one before 2031 only with supervised teaching and written wages that covered bills after travel. In the first year after 2031 I'd compare posted junior service work and apply where written pay and hours improved our position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household, with less pressure about how fast I had to learn the trade. I'd welcome years of supervised practice. I wouldn't imagine the reserve had grown while we were sitting here talking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would show the extra learning time was working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare what I could do correctly under the required checks with what the actual vacancies asked for. If I was just attending without gaining that ability, I'd ask the instructor what needed changing. I'd want useful work, not a growing pile of attendance papers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the apprenticeship paid less than the household needed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't leave the present job to show enthusiasm. I'd keep the wage and ask about other actual places. If a course charged a fee as well as losing wages, we'd need a different plan rather than raid the household reserve blindly.

say: I'd use **a decade** to build practical skill step by step while still asking for teaching now.
I wouldn't let a **later deadline** become a reason to leave the junior waiting for proper practice.
think: At **53 in 2036**, I would still need earnings without assuming retirement income or a vanished mortgage.
Current **curtain-order uncertainty** and the two-month reserve still make today's household budget a worry.
do: Maintain the **bill cut** and ask the supervisor for a paid practical development plan.
Accept a supervised **apprenticeship** before 2036 only with written wages covering household bills after travel.
Apply after 2036 for posted **repair roles** matching completed skills and offering workable written wages and hours.
feel: **Anxious** about present income, with more hope of becoming competent and no assumed retirement or children's support.
S4.quote: A decade gives more chances to learn, not a guarantee that teaching happens.
fieldNote: He retains **current household anxiety** instead of treating older children or future age as automatic relief from earning needs.
His **yearly check** requires actual learned tasks and better paid options, with an earlier search if promised teaching repeatedly fails.

steps.text: Maintain the optional sports-package cut to reduce household bills
Take supervised apprenticeship only with wages covering bills after travel
Apply for repair roles matching completed skills and offering workable written terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade means we can build a trade step by step, but we'd still need someone to teach each step. I'd ask for that teaching now while I was doing the work. A later deadline shouldn't become a reason to keep the junior waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 in 2036 and around 56 when the hands-on robots followed, still needing earnings unless our real finances said otherwise. I can't assume the children being older means the mortgage vanishes. And right now I'd still be worrying about the curtain orders and our two-month reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd keep the bill cut and seek a paid practice plan with the supervisor. I'd accept a supervised apprenticeship before 2036 only if its written wage covered household bills after travel. In the first year after 2036 I'd apply for posted repair roles matching skills I'd actually gained, comparing written pay and hours before any move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household today, but more hopeful about becoming a capable tradesman over time. I wouldn't use being in my fifties as a substitute for a retirement calculation we hadn't made. I'd want the next year's actual work to improve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you keep the decade from turning into waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look yearly at new tasks I could do correctly with the required checks and whether those skills brought better paid options. If the answer stayed nothing, I'd ask about other real places earlier. A decade gives more chances to learn, not a guarantee that teaching happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change plans for the children because of this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't make a decision about their studies today from one picture, or plan to live on their wages later. I'd tell them I was still learning and that useful work could mean asking for help. I'd rather show them an honest plan than pretend fathers never worry.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my junior hours could shrink before I'd learned enough to earn elsewhere. A supervised paid apprenticeship with a wage the household could live on would help more than encouragement to borrow for a course. Two months of savings gives us room to ask carefully, not room to stop earning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what the other household wage is doing before calling the electrician secure. My own pay packet isn't the only number on our kitchen table. I want to work our way through a change, but we need the whole set of numbers.

headlineQuote: Two months of savings gives us room to ask carefully, not room to stop earning.
portrait: **Adam, 43**, is a junior electrician with a vocational certificate, typical trade pay and practical skills still below the experienced crew's level.
He and **his partner** have two school-age children, a mortgage and two months of expenses saved, with curtain orders currently thin.
He uses **proven AI occasionally**, values apprenticeships and family help, and checks real supervised opportunities against household affordability.
Every scenario retains **household anxiety**; longer preparation helps learning without guaranteeing a second income, retirement or children's future financial support.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could shrink his junior hours before he learns enough to earn elsewhere.
whatWouldHelp: A **supervised paid apprenticeship** with livable household wages would help more than borrowing for a course.
